source.title: USGS Eaton 2025-01-08 v1.0 postfire debris-flow hazard assessment

scenario.soil_moisture_source: Open-Meteo archive API, models=era5_land, hourly soil_moisture_0_to_7cm (ECMWF ERA5-Land reanalysis, 0.1° grid), mean of the 24 UTC hours of the day before the storm, at the AOI center (34.1999, -118.0876)

analogue.note: The Station Fire (2009, San Gabriel front), 13 km from this fire's AOI center by the median of its observation points (the inventory's nearest fire with a recorded debris flow): 489 usable inventory records, 108 of them debris flows. Step 14 holds it out as its own fold, so its scores in model_eval.json are on unseen records (ROC AUC of the map's models: m1_refit 0.825, rf_extended 0.704). They score a past fire nearby, not this one. M1's form and its T variable were designed on the Staley et al. (2016) inventory, which holds every Station record, so this comparison may favour M1 recalibrated.

notes: These likelihoods are compared with USGS's assessment; nothing here scores them against outcomes. The data used here hold no observed debris-flow outcomes for the 2025 fires (USGS's inventory, 10.5066/P1R9VXC4, ends with 2024 fires), so agreement with USGS says how alike two models are on this fire, not which is closer to what happens.

Map columns: usgs_p_* is USGS's own M1 (Staley et al. 2017, published 15-minute coefficients), copied; m1_p_* is M1 recalibrated; rf_p_* is step 14's rf_extended, a random forest constrained to rise with rainfall, under this file's scenario. The MLPs are scored in step 14 but not mapped: nothing constrains them to rise with rainfall, and here mlp_extended's likelihood (at 4 decimals, as rf_p_* is written) would fall between consecutive design storms on 21 of 956 segments (largest fall 0.010).

M1 recalibrated (m1_p_*, coefficients in m1_recalibrated): M1's three-interaction logistic form refitted on all 7,639 usable inventory records (step 14's m1_refit), B = -3.25, Ct = 0.26, Cf = -0.018, Cs = 0.34, against the published B = -3.63, Ct = 0.41, Cf = 0.67, Cs = 0.70. Its likelihood rises with I15 wherever Ct·T + Cf·F + Cs·S > 0, which holds for 956 of 956 segments here (smallest 0.0601). Under one design storm every segment has the same R, so both M1 columns rank segments by Ct·T + Cf·F + Cs·S alone: m1's Spearman against USGS is the same under every storm (0.881), while its levels and classes move with I15.

m1_check is an implementation check of our M1 code, not a validation and not a result: M1 with the published coefficients (R = I15 × 0.25 h), recomputed from USGS's T, F and S, matches USGS's likelihoods for all 956 segments and 7 design storms to within 3e-16. It is not a map column.

Absolute likelihood levels depend on how each sub-inventory sampled non-events, not only on the watersheds: the observed debris-flow rate is 0.253 in the 1,320 Staley et al. (2016) records (the inventory M1's published coefficients were fitted on) and 0.098 in the other 6,319. M1 recalibrated averages 0.125 over all 7,639 usable records (0.151 on the Staley et al. (2016) records, 0.120 on the rest), and rf_extended was fitted on the same records. So the gap in level between usgs_p_* and the other two columns (mean at 24 mm/h: usgs 0.712, m1 0.161, rf 0.258) partly reflects which records each was fitted on. None of these levels is an observed rate for this fire.

Agreement with USGS over the seven design storms (agreement_by_i15): Spearman m1 0.881, rf 0.379–0.472; same likelihood class m1 0.014–0.139, rf 0.030–0.186. The usgs entries compare USGS with itself (1 by definition) and are there so every storm lists every map column.

The scenario is a choice. Only rf_p_* uses it: rf_extended takes days since fire and one antecedent soil-moisture value, the same for every segment, so the RF map depends on the scenario date and that one soil-moisture value; usgs_p_* and m1_p_* do not. Rule: the first local day after ignition with at least 25.4 mm (1 inch) of precipitation at the AOI center in ECMWF ERA5 (Open-Meteo archive, models=era5, grid point 34.25, -118.00; hourly accumulations, each for the hour ending at its GMT time stamp, summed into America/Los_Angeles calendar days): 2025-02-13, with 63.8 mm (peak hourly 6.0 mm/h). The wettest earlier day was 2025-02-06 with 14.4 mm, so any threshold above 14.4 mm and up to 63.8 mm picks the same day. 120 days searched, 0 with no value. A 0.25° hourly reanalysis only picks the date; it is not a 15-minute intensity, and the design storms set I15 instead.

days_since_fire = 37: from the CAL FIRE start (2025-01-08T02:18:00Z, local date 2025-01-07) to 2025-02-13, in calendar days like the inventory's StormStart − FireIgnitionDate. That is early in recovery compared with training: the usable inventory records have a median of 336 days, and only 950 of them (9 fires, 12 fire-storms, 198 debris flows) are from storms within 37 days of a fire; 857 of those are one storm, Thomas (2017) on 2018-01-09. What rf_extended does this early rests mostly on that one storm, so the level of rf_p_* under this scenario is an extrapolation from little data.

Antecedent soil moisture (0–7 cm) on 2025-02-12, the UTC day before the scenario date: 0.2891 m³/m³ at the AOI center's ERA5-Land cell (training median 0.2455). It is one value for every segment, as is days since fire, so both set the level of the RF map, not the ranking of segments; in training they varied between storms.

No map column uses spatial context; step 14 scores it only as the mlp_context variant, which is not mapped. For scale: on this network the mean distance from a segment's downstream end to the 5 nearest others has median 138 m (IQR 96–202 m), against 845 m (IQR 410–1,374 m) between the inventory's context neighbours, and here the neighbours include segments upstream and downstream on the same channel, whose watersheds nest.

Analogue: The Station Fire (2009, San Gabriel front), 13 km from this fire's AOI center by the median of its observation points (the inventory's nearest fire with a recorded debris flow): 489 usable inventory records, 108 of them debris flows. Step 14 holds it out as its own fold, so its scores in model_eval.json are on unseen records (ROC AUC of the map's models: m1_refit 0.825, rf_extended 0.704). They score a past fire nearby, not this one. M1's form and its T variable were designed on the Staley et al. (2016) inventory, which holds every Station record, so this comparison may favour M1 recalibrated.

T, F and S are USGS's values from its assessment inputs (its dNBR and burn-severity rasters, terrain and soil KF-factor), not computed from this project's AVIRIS-3 dNBR layer. area_km2 is USGS's Area (km²: the basin polygons' areas match it, median ratio 1.0023). usgs_hazard_24 is USGS's combined hazard class at 24 mm/h (likelihood and volume together; 1 low, 2 moderate, 3 high), copied as it is.

Likelihood classes are floor(p × 5) (0–20% … 80–100%); on USGS's likelihoods at 24 mm/h they reproduce USGS's own P_24_LG labels for 956 of 956 segments. Agreement, class counts and means use the values as written to debris_flow.geojson.

On the values as written, no segment's m1_p_* or rf_p_* falls between consecutive design storms (rf_extended by its constraint, M1 recalibrated by its form and positive slopes here); this step stops if one does. Nor does USGS's usgs_p_*.
USGS's median thresholds: median-thresholds.csv, 'Segments (mm)' row (equal to the median over the segments of I15_50 and I15_75 exactly).

Geometry: USGS's segments in lon/lat (urn:ogc:def:crs:OGC:1.3:CRS84), simplified at 2e-05° (~2 m) and rounded to 5 decimals. T, F, S, usgs_p_* and m1_p_* keep 8 decimals, and m1_recalibrated full precision, so both M1 columns can be recomputed from these files; rf_p_* and other values 4. The downstream end is a segment's last vertex: in all 861 pairs where one segment starts at another's end, the downstream one drains more area (861 of 861).
